pages.text: In the living room, a tiny box blinks—Wally the Wi‑Fi router. He’s ready to share internet signals around the home.
Wally sends invisible waves through the air. These waves are Wi‑Fi signals that nearby devices can listen to.
Phones and tablets connect to Wally. Then they can send data, like messages, pictures, and questions, to the internet.
A router is like a helper bridge. It passes data between your home devices and the bigger internet outside.
Walls and long distance can make signals weaker. Closer devices often get faster, stronger Wi‑Fi.
Sometimes too many devices share at once. Wally works hard, but waiting turns can help everyone connect smoothly.
A Wi‑Fi password is like a secret key. It helps keep strangers from joining your home network.
Grown-ups choose the password and settings. People stay in charge of what connects and when.
When the router restarts, the signal may pause. Then Wally wakes up and sends waves again.
At bedtime, Wally’s lights glow softly. Quiet signals keep ready, so devices can connect again tomorrow.
